senderIds.verification: Verifier verdict: unverifiable. I checked the cited source myself. The parser's doc comment lists 'Sender examples: SNB-AlAhli, SNB, AlAhliBank, الأهلي', and the test file uses sender = "SNB-AlAhli" in almost every case. The first version of that test (commit f88f21f, PR #255) used only 'SNB-AlAhli'. That PR says its test cases were taken 'from screenshot', which is weak sign the developer saw a real message, but it shows no screenshot and never says which sender appeared on the phone. The current test messages are openly synthetic: PR #708 calls them 'synthetic regression coverage', and merchants are named 'SYNTHETIC ...'. I found no independent confirmation. There is nothing on alahli.com (the site also failed the TLS check), no forum or X post, no news story, and no other repo outside PennyWise. Sourcegraph finds the exact string only in the PennyWise test file. Cashiro is derived from PennyWise, so it does not count as independent. The bank request in PennyWise issue #123 left the sender field blank. This is the most plausible current sender, but it rests on one developer's project. senderIds.verification: Verifier verdict: confirmed. The cited source checks out. The header of PennyWise AlRajhiBankParser.kt literally says 'Sender: AlRajhiBank', and every ParserTestCase in parser-core/src/test/kotlin/TestAlRajhiBankParser.kt uses 'AlRajhiBank'. Some of those tests are labelled SYNTHETIC, so the tests alone prove nothing. Better evidence is issue #207 in the same repo, opened in March 2026 by an outside end user (author_association NONE). It has eight real-looking Arabic and English Al Rajhi alerts with masked card and account fields. The template's sender field (placeholder 'e.g. AD-ICICIB') was filled with 'AlRajhiBank', wrapped in invisible right-to-left Unicode marks, which is typical of text copied from an Arabic-locale phone screen. This looks like a real observed sender, but it comes from the same project's user base, not the bank. Indirect support: a 2015 Saudi scam-SMS blog (personal blog post, July 2015; address withheld) lists fake lookalikes such as 'AIRajhBank', 'AlRajhBank_' and 'AIRaijhBank', which imitate this string. The bank's fraud page, its 2024 annual-report fraud section and SAMA notices do not name any sender, so 'official' is not justified. Advice: match without regard to case, and remember that Saudi carriers require sender-name registration but lookalike names exist. Evidence: GitHub repo pennywiseai-tracker [owner withheld], issue #207

senderIds.verification: Verifier verdict: unverifiable. I checked both cited sources myself. (1) masarif is a real Alinma-only app. Its welcome screen tells the user to type the sender 'as it appears in the Messages app (e.g. alinma)'. SettingsStore.kt sets DEFAULT_SENDER = "alinma", and the README says to leave it as 'alinma' and press verify. This is the only real-world signal. Its limits: it comes from one developer, it is phrased as an example, and InboxScanner.kt matches with address.contains(sender, ignoreCase = true). So it only shows that the sender contains 'alinma' in some casing (ALINMA, Alinma, AlinmaBank would all match). It does not show the exact string. (2) The PennyWise TestAlinmaBankParser.kt evidence is invented: placeholder merchants, **0000/**1234 suffixes, round amounts. The parser accepts any sender containing ALINMA or 'الإنماء'. The bank request it came from (issue #97) left the Sender field empty, showing only template placeholders. Do not cite it as evidence of the sender. (3) The researcher's formats note reads tidybox corpus.jsonl as 'sender alinma'. That is a misreading: the field is 'source', a provenance label next to values such as other GitHub users' handles and 'spamcsv', not an SMS address. The tidybox PR #17 also says its earlier Saudi sender list was 'written from memory'. Independent confirmation: none found. alinma.com (fraud-awareness page, SMS-alert news) does not name a sender ID. A 2015 blog lists 'ALINMA' in an unlabeled list mixed with spoofed variants, so it proves nothing. Recommendation: keep it as community, matched case-insensitively as a substring 'alinma', and record that the exact casing and full string are unverified. Evidence: GitHub repo masarif [owner withheld], file app/src/main/java/com/masarif/app/ui/screens/OnboardingScreen.kt

No independent confirmation was found: d360.com/en/fraud-awareness names no sender ID, the Cashiro tracker has no D360 entry, and web searches returned nothing. PR #708 uses synthetic samples and adds nothing. All the evidence comes from one reporter, so 'community' is the right level, not 'official'. Match the sender ignoring case.
